title: RATE LIMITER
subtitle: Every public API needs one, and the obvious implementation has a race condition.
footer: DDIA: Ch 7 lost update · Ch 6 shard by key   ·   Similar: URL shortener · Business discovery · News feed · News aggregator

items: Counting per server gives each client N times its limit; the counter must be shared, usually in Redis.
Read-then-write on a shared counter races. Do the refill, check and decrement atomically in one Lua script.
Decide what happens when Redis is down: allow traffic (fail-open) or block it (fail-closed), per endpoint.
Limit requests per client (user, IP, API key) by configurable rules
Return 429 with Retry-After and rate-limit headers
Adds < 10ms latency
Accurate across many API servers
Highly available (choose fail-open vs fail-closed)
1M requests/sec total
1M req/s = 1M Redis ops/s; one Redis node does ~100k ops/s, so a ~10–20 shard Redis Cluster keyed by client.
10M active keys × 100B ≈ 1GB of memory.

blocks.text: Naive: each API server counts in local memory. With 50 servers, a client gets 50× the limit.

items: Centralize counters in Redis. But GET then SET from two servers races: both see 99/100 and both allow.
A Lua script runs refill + check + decrement atomically inside single-threaded Redis, in one round trip, with no race.
Rules come from a config store cached in each gateway. Decide failure mode: fail-open for normal APIs, fail-closed for login and payments.
Which algorithm?
Token bucket (capacity = burst, refill = sustained rate) is the industry default.
Race between servers?
Read-modify-write is a lost update (DDIA Ch 7). Atomic Lua or INCR + EXPIRE inside Redis fixes it.
Redis is down?
Fall back to local limits (limit ÷ N servers). Fail-open vs fail-closed is a product decision per endpoint.
Very hot client?
One key lands on one shard. Give each server a local allowance and sync periodically, trading accuracy for load.
Counters in Postgres: 1M writes/sec of throwaway data.
Adding parts before a number shows they are needed.
Ignoring retries, timeouts and crashes.
